newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Rabat leads hunt for "$3 bln drug" gang. [CORRECTED 17:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Rabat leads hunt for "$3 bln drug" gang. [CORRECTED 17:25 GMT]

text.p: Police and drug experts in half a dozen Europen countries are checking leads for the network and planned destination of six tonnes of cocaine seized in Morocco with a potential treated value of around $3 billion.

Moroccan Interior Minister Driss Basri told Reuters on Monday that an international warrant had been issued for the arrest of two Spaniards. British police were investigating "the Englishmen implicated in this affair", he said.
While the authorities did not have a specific street value, Basri said: "The first estimate goes from practically $600 million, and when you multiply by 20 it goes to around $3 billion dollars..."
These estimates, on a formula used by drug experts, set a first figure with a coefficient of 'one' on untreated cocaine.
"Then if it is transformed into the final stage you have to multiply its current value by 20," the minister said.
German, French, Portuguese, Italian and American experts were helping the Moroccan inquiry in which four Colombians and a German have been arrested, he said.
Besides the hunt for other traffickers, Morocco and experts from other countries were looking at ways to destroy the drug.
This, Basri pledged, would be in public as part of Morocco's commitment to battling drug trafficking.

"German services particularly" were helping look at the latest technology to ensure complete destruction of the drug through "incineration, which is, I think, the first (such operation) in the world of such an important quantity of cocaine", he added.

According to Moroccan authorities, a four-man English crew sailed the boat to Agadir, southern Morocco after it was sold in England for $395,000. They left Morocco in April and the boat, Duanas, was later taken over by four Colombians.
The four Colombians (corrects from Britons) and two Spaniards sailed to a rendezvous with a ship, Tassan, from Cartagena, Colombia.
At 5 p.m. on June 11, they took on board the cocaine only to have to jettison it after engine trouble near the Moroccan coast.

The Duanas, which had been heading for Spain and Portugal, was towed into the Moroccan port of Kenitra, 35 km (20 miles) north of Rabat. The Spanish nationals fled. The Colombians were later arrested and a German national who came to Morocco looking for the boat was also arrested.
"The German came to Morocco to pay for the stopover of the boat," Basri said.
An anti-drug unit official named the German as Karl Peter Weiss, born in 1947. He had done various jobs, including hotel work. His role was to pay for the repairs, said the official.
"So when he came and asked about the crew, who had already been arrested, he was arrested," he added.
The four Colombians were named as Santander Murillo Gonzales, 60, George Isaac Vasquez, 40, Flores Sanchez, born in 1958, and Harold Sanchez Paz, born the following year.

Murillo Gonzales, who had skippered boats from 1988, flew with Isaac Vasquez, a seaman-electrician, to Casablanca, Morocco from London, and went to Agadir to take over as captain of the Duanas. Both men had Equadorian passports.
Flores Sanches had skippered various boats upto 1992 from when he had been without work, the official said. Sanchez Paz had also been unemployed for the past year.

Basri said the latest package of cocaine, 85 kg, was washed up near the town of Safi just four days ago. Since June 21 when the first packet arrived, hundreds turned up over a 200 km (125 miles) stretch of Atlantic coastline.

He insisted that Morocco was a victim of the drug runners and wanted "moral and material" compensation from those implicated. How this could be done would be raised at an international meeting of drug experts which Morocco planned to hold on tackling the drug trade.
